title: AC Repair Midtown, Houston | AC Repair Houston
description: Condo towers beside 1920s houses near Main and Lamar, where getting duct from the air handler to the room is the hard part.
intro: Midtown stacks two kinds of cooling work on top of each other. On one side there are condo towers and apartment buildings sharing plant on a roof, and on the other there are some of the earliest twentieth century houses in Houston, sitting a short drive from Lamar and Main with brick walls and rooms that were framed for coal heat. In those older shells the ducts cannot go where a modern system wants them to go, and that routing is where most of the work gets decided.
localAngle: The houses along Main and Lamar date to the 1900s through the 1920s, built tight to the street with heavy masonry and almost no attic worth running duct through. Cooling added to one of these is a routing puzzle: the air handler lands in a basement or a closet, and the supply has to find a path through a wall that already holds wiring and plumbing. Taller buildings sit beside them with fan coil units in ceiling cavities and rooftop machinery above. Add apartment conversions where a balcony became a room and the capacity plan changes fast.
commonCalls: Duct runs in converted 1920s houses that no longer reach the rooms they were built for
Fan coil units in condo ceilings that drip onto the floor below when the pan overflows
Rooftop equipment serving a tower where only some floors are cooling
Systems that never were big enough for a house that has been added to twice
Condensers and line sets that a building has no convenient pad for

faqs.q: My house is from the 1920s. How does anyone add central air to it?
faqs.a: By routing around what is already there. In these masonry shells the realistic options are a compact unit in the basement or a rear closet with a line set that runs through an existing chase, or a ductless head per room where there is no path for duct at all. Opening a wall to run new duct is possible but it is a bigger job than the equipment itself. The technician who comes out should walk the house and show you the route before quoting a system.

faqs.q: My condo is fine until a hot week. What changes on a hot week?
faqs.a: The building plant gets loaded and so does the outdoor equipment feeding the fan coil in your ceiling. If the building's chillers are already at their limit, your unit is working against a supply air that is warmer than it should be. Separately, a fan coil in a ceiling cavity works harder in humid weather, and a restricted return in that cavity makes it run long without conditioning the room properly. The fix depends on whether the shortfall is at the plant or at your unit.

faqs.q: Do I need permission before work on the exterior of my building?
faqs.a: If you live in a condominium or in a building with a homeowners association, the exterior usually needs approval before a new condenser location, a fence screen or a pad change goes in. A conversion of a historic house can also involve landmark review if the building is designated. That process runs on the building side rather than the HVAC side, so it is worth starting before the equipment is ordered rather than after.

faqs.q: The room over my garage is the hottest in the house. What is going on?
faqs.a: A room built over a garage usually sits outside the conditioned envelope, with the sun on the roof and no duct run reaching it. In a converted or reworked house it may be getting cool air from a distant register and recirculating it. Two options work here: ductless heads on that zone, or running the existing duct circuit out to it with the returns repositioned so the system actually pulls air from that room. Either way the diagnosis starts with checking what the return side is doing.

faqs.q: Is it worth replacing the ductwork while I am changing the system anyway?
faqs.a: On these older shells it usually is, because the ductwork is the part that cannot be reached later. A house from the 1900s through the 1920s with heavy masonry walls and almost no attic space cannot take a new run without opening structure, and the first time that happens it is worth running the circuit properly rather than hanging another length of flex duct off the existing one. What moves the price is the route. Whether the path goes through a basement ceiling or a closet chase, whether the wall has to be opened and patched, and how many branches the new layout serves all change the job. A technician should walk the house and mark the route before any of that is priced.

faqs.q: Water is dripping from my ceiling. Is it coming from the unit above me?
faqs.a: In a tower it often is. Fan coil units sit in a ceiling cavity, and the condensate pan under the coil has a float that shuts the unit down when the drain cannot keep up. When the drain line partly blocks, the pan fills and the overflow finds the gap around the pipe chase, which puts the water in the ceiling of the unit below. That is why the leak shows up in an apartment that has no equipment of its own in that space. The work has to start on the floor above, which is why this is worth raising with building management rather than treating as a ceiling repair in your own unit.

_faqsNote: 6 FAQs. The 1920s masonry shells, the ceiling cavities in the towers, the room over the garage and the tight lots carry the local weight.
